clinicalPearls: Caused by spirochetes of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato group (also called Borreliella spp.), transmitted by Ixodes ricinus complex ticks; B. burgdorferi sensu stricto is the predominant cause in the United States, while B. afzelii, B. garinii, and B. bavariensis also occur in Europe and Asia. (p.1448-1449)

Staged illness: stage 1 (early localized) presents with erythema migrans (EM); stage 2 (early disseminated) may follow with secondary skin lesions, neurologic involvement (meningitis, cranial neuritis, radiculoneuritis), carditis with atrioventricular block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain; stage 3 (late/persistent) typically manifests as intermittent arthritis and, rarely, chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis. (p.1448-1449)

EM begins after an incubation period of roughly 3-32 days as a red macule or papule at the bite site that expands into a large annular lesion, often with a bright red outer border and partial central clearing; common sites include the thigh, groin, and axilla, and the lesion is warm but usually not painful. (p.1451)
Approximately 20% of patients do NOT develop the characteristic EM skin lesion, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. (p.1451)

Cardiac involvement occurs in about 8% of patients within weeks of onset; the most common abnormality is fluctuating atrioventricular block (first-degree, Wenckebach, or complete heart block), and most cardiac involvement lasts only a few weeks. (p.1451)

About 15% of untreated patients develop frank neurologic abnormalities after weeks to months; the typical U.S. pattern is fluctuating meningitis with facial palsy (cranial neuritis, often the facial nerve, sometimes bilateral) and peripheral radiculoneuropathy. CSF in U.S. neuroborreliosis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (~100 cells/uL) with elevated protein and normal or slightly low glucose. (p.1451)

In Europe and Asia the characteristic first neurologic sign is radicular pain followed by CSF pleocytosis (meningopolyneuritis or Bannwarth's syndrome), often without meningeal or encephalitic signs. (p.1451)

Lyme arthritis (stage 3) develops in about 60% of untreated U.S. patients months after onset; the typical pattern is intermittent oligoarticular attacks in large joints, especially the knees. Joint fluid white cell counts range widely (500-110,000/uL, average ~25,000/uL), mostly neutrophils, and rheumatoid factor and ANA tests are usually negative. (p.1451)

Most patients experience early symptoms during summer, reflecting transmission by nymphal Ixodes ticks; the tick must usually remain attached for at least about 24 hours for transmission of B. burgdorferi. (p.1449-1450)

Lyme disease is the most common vector-borne infection in the United States and Europe; in the U.S. more than 30,000 cases are reported annually but true cases are estimated at about 476,000 per year. (p.1450)

Posttreatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) affects roughly 10% of treated patients (reported figures vary widely) with persistent subjective pain, neurocognitive symptoms, or fatigue; there is NO evidence these symptoms reflect active infection, and randomized trials show repeated antibiotic courses do not help and are not recommended. (p.1451-1453)

Reinfection can occur after EM treated with antibiotics because the immune response after early infection is not protective; however, patients who develop an expanded immune response over months (e.g., those with Lyme arthritis) have protective immunity for years and rarely become reinfected. (p.1454)
Maternal-fetal transmission of B. burgdorferi appears to occur rarely if at all; standard therapy is recommended for pregnant women. (p.1453)
No Lyme disease vaccine is currently commercially available; the previously marketed vaccine was discontinued by its manufacturer. (p.1454)
harrison.pathophysiology: B. burgdorferi is a fastidious microaerophilic spirochete with an unusually small genome and more than 100 predicted lipoproteins, mostly plasmid-encoded and displayed on the outer membrane to interact with host and tick. It expresses outer-surface protein A (OspA) in the tick midgut and upregulates OspC during migration to the salivary gland, where OspC binds the tick salivary protein Salp15 (required for mammalian infection). After injection into skin the organism downregulates OspC and upregulates the antigenically variable VlsE lipoprotein, then may migrate outward to produce EM and spread hematogenously or via lymphatics to skin, nervous system, heart, and joints. Its only known virulence factors are surface proteins that attach to host proteins, integrins, glycosaminoglycans, or glycoproteins (e.g., plasminogen binding aids tissue spread; complement regulators such as Factor H protect against lysis; decorin-binding proteins bind collagen-associated decorin, possibly explaining alignment with collagen fibrils). The host mounts innate and adaptive responses producing proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IFN-gamma) and opsonizing antibodies; immune mechanisms eventually control disseminated infection even without antibiotics, though spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. Postinfectious (antibiotic-refractory) Lyme arthritis is not due to persistent infection (culture and PCR of synovium are uniformly negative after antibiotics) but to a dysregulated, excessive proinflammatory response with very high IFN-gamma, host genetic factors (HLA-DRB1*0401, TLR1 1805GG polymorphism), and autoimmune responses to vascular and extracellular matrix autoantigens.
additionalDifferentials: Uninfected tick bite (red papule that expands little) versus EM
Cellulitis (e.g., streptococcal) or allergic reaction to tick saliva when a lesion expands rapidly
Erythema multiforme in patients with secondary annular lesions (but mucosal blistering and palm/sole involvement are NOT features of B. burgdorferi infection)
Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI) from Amblyomma americanum bites, an EM-like lesion whose cause is not yet identified
Peripheral spondyloarthropathy or pauciarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis versus oligoarticular Lyme arthritis
Bell's palsy (herpes simplex virus type 1) and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella-zoster virus) versus Lyme facial palsy
Chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia versus late-stage Lyme disease or PTLDS
infectionMimics: Babesiosis (Babesia microti), co-transmitted by I. scapularis, causing an influenza-like illness with thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia
Human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum), which may cause leukopenia/thrombocytopenia and can elicit a false-positive IgM response to B. burgdorferi
Borrelia miyamotoi relapsing fever, co-transmitted by I. scapularis
Borrelia mayonii and Ehrlichia muris-like agent infections in the upper midwestern United States
Powassan virus (deer tick virus) infection, which may be fatal
Ehrlichia chaffeensis transmitted by Amblyomma americanum in the same regions as STARI
nonInfectiousMimics: Peripheral spondyloarthropathy / juvenile idiopathic arthritis (for the arthritis presentation)
additionalInvestigations: Two-tier serology: conventional approach with ELISA followed by Western blot for equivocal/positive results, or a modified two-test approach using two enzyme immunoassays (e.g., whole-sonicate ELISA followed by VlsE C6 peptide IgG ELISA) that dispenses with the Western blot
IgM and IgG responses during early infection, ideally in paired acute- and convalescent-phase sera (~20-30% positive in acute phase, ~70-80% during convalescence)
After 4-8 weeks, the IgG response by ELISA and Western blot has very high sensitivity and specificity (~99%); a single IgG test is then usually sufficient
Western blot band criteria: IgM positive if 2 of 3 bands (23, 39, 41 kDa); IgG positive if 5 of 10 bands (18, 23, 28, 30, 39, 41, 45, 58, 66, 93 kDa)

PCR of joint fluid for B. burgdorferi DNA (its main PCR application; superior to culture later in disease, though DNA may persist after killing so it does NOT confirm active infection or therapy adequacy)
Culture of B. burgdorferi in Barbour-Stoenner-Kelly (BSK) medium, used mainly in research and positive chiefly early (EM biopsy, occasionally plasma or CSF)
CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein in neuroborreliosis
Peripheral blood smear and blood PCR to evaluate for tick-borne co-infections; standard blood counts may give clues (cytopenias)
redFlags: High-degree (third-degree) atrioventricular block or PR interval >0.3 s in carditis, warranting IV therapy and cardiac monitoring
Severe objective neurologic abnormalities (e.g., meningitis, encephalitis, severe neuroborreliosis)
Optic nerve involvement in children from inflammation or raised intracranial pressure, which may lead to blindness
Borrelial encephalomyelitis/leukoencephalitis (rare, mainly B. garinii in Europe) with spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction
Suspected tick-borne co-infection (e.g., babesiosis, anaplasmosis, Powassan virus), which can cause severe or fatal illness, especially in the very young or elderly
harrison.prognosis: Response to treatment is best when given early in the disease; later treatment remains effective but the convalescent period may be longer. Eventually most patients recover with minimal or no residual deficits. Even without antibiotics, innate and adaptive immunity usually control disseminated infection within weeks to months, though untreated spirochetes may persist in localized niches for years. A small percentage develop persistent postinfectious arthritis or, rarely, chronic encephalopathy or polyneuropathy, and about 10% have PTLDS, which usually improves over months but may last years.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative serologic test excludes acute Lyme disease - serology may be negative during the first several weeks (early seronegativity), so diagnosis of early Lyme disease is clinical
Missing the diagnosis because of atypical EM morphology or because ~20% of patients never develop EM
Relying on a positive IgM result alone in illness lasting more than 2 months - such an isolated IgM is likely false-positive and should not support the diagnosis
Misusing or misinterpreting IgM Western blots, a recognized cause of incorrect Lyme diagnoses in patients with other illnesses
Using serology as a screening test in patients with nonspecific pain or fatigue (low pretest probability), where a false-positive result is more likely than a true-positive
Interpreting persisting seropositivity (including VlsE C6 and IgM responses, which can persist for years after therapy) as evidence of active, recent, or recurrent infection

Treating persistent subjective symptoms as active infection - 'chronic Lyme disease' equated with chronic B. burgdorferi infection is a misnomer, and repeated/prolonged antibiotic courses lack benefit and carry documented harm
Using PCR positivity in joint fluid to judge active infection or adequacy of therapy, since DNA may persist for weeks after spirochetal killing
harrison.severityClassification: Staged clinical classification per Harrison: Stage 1 - early localized infection (erythema migrans at the bite site). Stage 2 - early disseminated infection (secondary annular skin lesions, neurologic involvement such as meningitis/cranial neuritis/radiculoneuritis/peripheral neuritis, carditis with atrioventricular nodal block, and migratory musculoskeletal pain). Stage 3 - late/persistent infection (intermittent or persistent arthritis, and rarely chronic encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, or acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans). For diagnostic/testing purposes, the American College of Physicians algorithm stratifies by pretest probability: high (EM - treat empirically without serology), intermediate (e.g., oligoarticular arthritis - test and treat if positive), and low (nonspecific symptoms - neither test nor treat).
management: First-line oral doxycycline for erythema migrans and early disease, with amoxicillin or cefuroxime as alternatives in pregnancy or young children
Intravenous ceftriaxone or penicillin for neuroborreliosis, high-grade atrioventricular block or other severe disseminated disease
Oral doxycycline for Lyme arthritis, reserving parenteral therapy or a repeat course for persistent synovitis
Cardiac monitoring with temporary pacing support for symptomatic high-grade heart block
Symptomatic measures such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for arthralgia and eye protection for facial-nerve palsy
Tick-bite prevention, prompt tick removal and post-exposure doxycycline prophylaxis after high-risk bites
Reassure and monitor recovery, since most patients resolve fully and prolonged antibiotic courses are not indicated for lingering non-specific symptoms
